text: This lab is a worked written scenario: audit a real company's sprawled facilities role hierarchy, then redesign it using the least-privilege and anti-sprawl principles from Lesson 2.

Three roles accumulated over three years: facilities_viewer with read access, facilities_admin with read, write, and create, and facilities_super_admin, built for one person's one-off project, adding delete rights. The names imply a clean hierarchy. The actual grants, as you'll see, don't.

The audit ignores role names and reads actual grants directly. facilities_admin's Contains Roles field is empty — it duplicates facilities_viewer's read access with its own separate ACL grants instead of inheriting it, even though both roles were clearly meant to build on each other. And a quick interview turns up the second problem: the one person facilities_super_admin was built for left the company fourteen months ago, and nobody ever revoked or re-evaluated the role since.

The redesign collapses to two roles. facilities_user becomes the single source of read access. facilities_admin is rebuilt so its Contains Roles field lists facilities_user, and its own direct grants shrink to only what's additional: write and create. facilities_super_admin is retired outright — its real use case ended over a year ago, and reviving it later, if the need ever returns, means building a narrow role on purpose, not reusing a role that had become a catch-all.

Notice what the fix didn't touch: not a single ACL's logic, not one field-level rule from Lesson 1's layers. The entire fix was role-hierarchy hygiene — eliminating a duplicated grant path and retiring a role whose reason for existing had quietly expired. That's exactly why Lesson 2 insisted on periodic review of the whole hierarchy, not just careful design of each new role in isolation.
Chapter 2 goes deeper into ACLs themselves, starting with Lesson 4: how multiple ACLs on a single table actually resolve, in depth, beyond the basics.
